thread.title: Afghanistan's Musical Tradition in Danger of Dying Out
thread.title_full: Afghanistan's Musical Tradition in Danger of Dying Out

author: ELENA BECATOROS - Associated Press
title: Afghanistan's Musical Tradition in Danger of Dying Out
text:
• The Taliban banned music in Afghanistan in 2022, allowing only religious music.
• The ban is enforced by the Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice.
• Many musicians fled the country after the takeover.
• Those who remained sent their instruments abroad or hid them to save them from being smashed by authorities.
• Music shops in Kabul's old city now sell other wares, excluding musical instruments.
• Musicians lost their livelihoods overnight.
• Some musicians continue to play in secret, despite the danger.
• A musician pulled out his hand-carved wooden rubab and played in a small home in Kabul.
• He vowed to continue playing as long as he is alive.
• A singer echoed the musician's determination, saying music will continue to be played in secret or in dreams.
• The singer had performed at concerts and celebrations before the takeover, but now hides his instruments.
• He believes music gave him life and brought him fame and recognition.
• The musician who taught music at a school and owned a traditional musical instrument shop lost his business after the takeover.
• He now barely makes 100 afghanis ($1.50) as a manual laborer.
• The singer spent two years unemployed before starting a small business with the help of friends.
• Underground performances have become too dangerous due to government agents actively searching for musicians to arrest.
• A gathering the singer attended was raided by the vice and virtue police after someone took photos and sent them to the authorities.
• The rubab player learned how to play from his father and plans to teach his eldest son.
• He believes the tradition must continue and that music is a legacy from his father and grandfather.
• The singer believes music is inseparable from Afghan society and culture.
summary: The Taliban who seized power in 2021 have prohibited anything but religious music — unaccompanied vocal chanting — with the ban enforced by the feared morality police of the Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice. The music shops in Kucha-e-Kharabat, the neighborhood in Kabul's old city where many musicians lived, now sell other wares, from food and groceries to clothes and household goods. He, too, has hidden his instruments: a rubab, a harmonium, a flute, a tabla — traditional Afghan hand drums — and a keyboard.
